title: How to Preach the Old Testament Prophets
subtitle: A guide to preaching the Old Testament prophets, handling oracles of judgment and hope, historical context, and the prophetic voice without turning sermons into bad news.

sections.title: The Prophets Were Not Predicting Your Headlines
sections.body:
Most preaching of the prophets goes wrong in the first minute. It treats them as a code to be cracked.

We open Isaiah or Ezekiel and start matching verses to current events, helicopters in Joel, nations in Ezekiel aligned with this morning's news. The prophet becomes a fortune teller and the sermon becomes a puzzle. This is not what these men were doing. A prophet was a covenant prosecutor. He stood in the courtroom of a broken relationship and read the charges. He called a forgetful people back to the God who had bound himself to them. The prediction was always in service of the indictment, and the indictment was always in service of return.

Before you can preach a prophet, you have to put down the decoder ring. These books are not mainly about the future. They are about a people who forgot who they were, and a God who would not let them stay that way.

sections.title: You Cannot Skip the History
sections.body:
A prophetic oracle without its history is a sword swinging in the dark. It will cut someone, but not where it was aimed.

Amos thundered at a nation fat with prosperity and rotten with injustice. Jeremiah preached collapse to a city that could not imagine it. Habakkuk argued with God about an invasion he could not square with God's goodness. Pull the words out of those rooms and they become free-floating threats you can point at anyone. Anchor them, and they become precise. Amos is not yelling at the poor. He is yelling at the comfortable who trampled the poor and went to worship afterward. That precision only exists if you have done the historical work first.

Spend the study learning the king, the crisis, the sin being named. Who is this aimed at, and why now. Until you can answer that, you are not ready to ask what it means for the people in front of you. The history is not background. It is the aim.

sections.title: Recover the Prophetic Imagination
sections.body:
The prophets did two things at once, and a preacher who can only do one of them has missed the calling.

They dismantled and they dreamed. They tore down the false world the powerful had built, the religion that covered injustice, the peace that was no peace, and in the same breath they painted a world that did not yet exist, swords into plowshares, a valley of dry bones standing up, a shoot from a dead stump. Walter Brueggemann called this the prophetic imagination, the refusal to accept the present arrangement as the final word. The prophet grieves what is and announces what will be. Most of our preaching does neither. It manages. It soothes. It keeps the present arrangement comfortable.

To preach a prophet you have to be willing to name the thing in your own room, the idol your own people are protecting, and then to hold out a future so vivid your people ache for it. That is not a technique you add. It is a nerve you recover.

sections.title: Never Leave Them in the Rubble
sections.body:
The prophets indict, but indictment is never the destination. The pattern is judgment and then hope, and you betray the book if you stop at the judgment.

Nearly every prophet follows the same arc. The charges are read, the verdict falls, the people are broken open, and then, almost unbearably, the promise comes. After the desolation, a remnant. After the exile, a return. After the dry bones, breath. The God who tears is the God who heals, and he tears in order to heal. A preacher who only ever delivers the bad news has turned the prophets into a hammer. A preacher who skips the bad news has turned them into a greeting card. The text refuses both.

Preach the full arc. Let your people feel the weight of what they have done, and then let them hear the thing the prophets could barely believe themselves, that the same God who pronounced the ruin had already planned the rescue. Do not resolve it too cleanly. But do not leave them in the rubble. The prophet never did.

sections.title: The Promise Had a Name
sections.body:
The prophets reached toward a future they could not see clearly. We preach knowing what it was.

The servant who would be pierced for our transgressions. The new covenant written on the heart. The king from Bethlehem, the Spirit poured out on all flesh, the day God himself would shepherd the scattered sheep. The prophets strained toward a hope that stayed just beyond their sight, and the New Testament tells us they were searching for the grace that came in Christ. When you preach a prophet, you are standing on the near side of the thing they longed for. Their hope is your history.

This does not let you rush past the prophet to Jesus in a cheap leap. Preach the oracle in its own world first. But do not abandon your people in the Old Testament dark, as though the promise never came. Show them the prophet reaching, and then show them the hand that reached back.
